consultation:
Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s vision or eyes.
Parent: Our son has myopia, which means he has difficulty seeing distant objects clearly. We've had to get him glasses to help correct this issue, and it's been a significant adjustment for him to wear them all the time.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child's hearing or ears.
Parent: Sometimes we notice he doesn't always respond when we call him, even when we're sure he can hear us. It's not a consistent problem, but it happens often enough that we've started to look into whether there might be an underlying issue with his hearing or perhaps an attention span concern.

Doctor: Please tell us about the problems with your child’s teeth.
Parent: Due to some structural issues with his teeth, he needs more frequent dental visits than most children. This has meant a lot of trips to the dentist for preventative care and treatment.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s heart.
Parent: Unfortunately, our child was born with a septal defect. This is a hole in the wall between the chambers of his heart. We work closely with cardiologists to monitor this condition and ensure it doesn't cause further complications.

Doctor: Please tell us about any neurological problem your child has (brain, nerves, muscle tone, fits).
Parent: Developmentally, he's been slower to reach certain milestones like walking or sitting compared to his peers. While he eventually achieves these milestones, the delay has required patience and additional support from physical therapists.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's kidneys.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s immune system (ability to fight infection and vaccination responses).
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child’s gastrointestinal system (feeding, stomach, bowel).
Parent: Feeding has been a challenge. He has difficulties with certain textures and tastes that make meal times stressful. We've worked with nutritionists to develop strategies to make feeding easier and less frustrating for him.

Doctor: Please use this box to tell us about any other medical problems that you haven’t been able to mention above.
Parent: Additionally, our son has short fingers on both hands. This affects his ability to grasp certain objects and perform tasks that require fine motor skills. We're exploring options for adaptive tools and therapies to help him overcome these challenges.
report:
# CLINICAL PATIENT REPORT

## 1) RESPIRATORY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a septal defect, a hole in the wall between the chambers of his heart, which requires monitoring by cardiologists to prevent further complications.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: According to the clinical reference guidelines, around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes, some of which may require surgery or monitoring.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has difficulties with feeding due to issues with certain textures and tastes, making meal times stressful. Strategies have been developed with nutritionists to make feeding easier.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Many babies with KBG syndrome have feeding difficulties, and some require short-term nasogastric tube feeding to supplement oral feeds. A very small number of children have required longer-term tube feeding.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has developmental delays, including slower achievement of milestones like walking or sitting, and has required additional support from physical therapists.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Developmental delay has been reported in almost all children with KBG syndrome, with the degree of delay ranging from mild to severe. Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, which typically respond to anti-epileptic treatments.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient sometimes does not respond when called, suggesting potential issues with hearing or attention span.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: A significant proportion of people with KBG syndrome have recurrent otitis media or glue ear, leading to conductive hearing loss, and many have required multiple grommet insertions or hearing aids.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has myopia (nearsightedness) and wears glasses to correct this issue.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: People with KBG syndrome are more likely to have vision problems such as astigmatism, short- or long-sightedness, and squint. Regular eyesight reviews are recommended.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has structural issues with his teeth, requiring more frequent dental visits for preventative care and treatment.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Many people with KBG syndrome have dental concerns, including weak enamel, and require regular dental check-ups. Large front teeth are a common feature of the syndrome.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Children with KBG syndrome typically need extra help in school, and many attend mainstream primary school but may transfer to special schooling or remain in mainstream schools with Educational Health Care Plans (EHCP) for secondary education.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has developmental delays and requires additional support.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: People with KBG syndrome often have behavioural differences, such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), ADHD, or anxiety, and may require medication or therapy.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has short fingers on both hands, affecting his ability to grasp objects and perform tasks requiring fine motor skills.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Some people with KBG syndrome have skeletal anomalies, including an unusual structure of their spinal bones, short fingers (brachydactyly), and curvature of the 5th fingers (clinodactyly). Regular skeletal reviews are recommended.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
* Regular dental check-ups to monitor and address dental concerns.
* Regular hearing reviews to age 5 to detect and manage any hearing issues.
* Eyesight (ophthalmology) review to correct vision problems.
* Cardiac review, including echo and ECG, following diagnosis to monitor heart conditions.
* Consideration of a skeletal review (X-ray of the wrist, hip, spine, and skull) in children following diagnosis to identify any skeletal anomalies.
* Monitoring of growth velocity, with referral for endocrine investigations if height is below the 2nd centile.
* Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and behavioural therapy as needed to support developmental delays and other challenges.

a) How this affects the patient: N/A

## 1) RESPIRATORY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a structural abnormality in his heart, which is being monitored by a cardiologist.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Approximately 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experienced feeding difficulties as a baby, including spitting up and showing signs of discomfort after eating.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Many babies with KBG syndrome have feeding difficulties, and some require short-term nasogastric tube feeding to supplement oral feeds.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences episodes where he stares off into space for a few seconds before snapping back to normal, and has delayed speech.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and some may experience developmental delay and behavioral differences such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) or ADHD.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient had otitis media as a younger child and has ongoing issues with hearing, including potential conductive hearing loss.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: A significant proportion of people with KBG syndrome have recurrent otitis media or glue ear, which can cause conductive hearing loss.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient complains of blurry vision, especially when reading or watching TV, and may have issues with how his eyes focus.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: People with KBG syndrome are more likely to have vision problems such as astigmatism, short- or long-sightedness, and squint.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has difficulty chewing harder foods like meat or nuts and tends to avoid them or ask for them to be cut into smaller pieces.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Many people with KBG syndrome have dental concerns, including weak enamel, and require regular dental check-ups.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient's speech is somewhat delayed compared to his peers, and he is working through ongoing challenges with his therapists and doctors.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Children with KBG syndrome typically need extra help in school, and many go to mainstream primary school, but may transfer to special schooling or remain in mainstream schools with Educational Health Care Plans (EHCP).

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences episodes where he stares off into space, and has delayed speech.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: People with KBG syndrome often have behavioral differences such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), ADHD, or anxiety.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Some people with KBG syndrome have an unusual structure of their spinal bones, which can give rise to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis), and may have short fingers (brachydactyly) with a curvature of the 5th fingers (clinodactyly).

* Regular dental check-ups to monitor dental health and address any concerns.
* Regular hearing reviews to age 5 to monitor for conductive hearing loss.
* Eyesight (ophthalmology) review to address any vision problems.
* Cardiac review, including echo and ECG, to monitor the structural abnormality in the heart.
* Consider a skeletal review (X-ray of the wrist, hip, spine, and skull) to monitor for any skeletal abnormalities.
* Monitor growth velocity and consider referral for endocrine investigations if height is below the 2nd centile.
* Consider physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and behavioral therapy to address ongoing challenges.

b) How this affects others with the syndrome: A significant proportion of people with KBG syndrome have recurrent otitis media or glue ear, which can cause conductive hearing loss.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient complains of blurry vision, especially when trying to read or watch TV, and is planning to get his eyes checked soon.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: People with KBG syndrome are more likely to have vision problems such as astigmatism, short- or long-sightedness, and squint.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences difficulty chewing harder foods, such as meat or crunchy fruits, but manages soft foods like pasta or mashed potatoes.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: As well as large front teeth, there can be a variety of other dental concerns, including weak enamel, and careful brushing is very important.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient takes a bit more time to hit developmental milestones, and the family keeps track of his progress closely.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Children with KBG syndrome typically need extra help in school, and most go to a mainstream primary school, but may transfer to special schooling or remain in mainstream schools with Educational Health Care Plans.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences developmental delays and takes more time to hit milestones.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: People with KBG syndrome often have behavioural differences, such as autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, or anxiety, and may require medication or therapy.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Some people with KBG syndrome have an unusual structure of their spinal bones, which can give rise to an increased curvature of the spine, and many have short fingers with a curvature of the 5th fingers.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
* Regular dental check-ups to monitor dental concerns and prevent complications.
* Regular hearing reviews to age 5 to monitor hearing and address any concerns.
* Eyesight review to assess vision and address any concerns.
* Cardiac review, including echo and ECG, to monitor heart condition and adjust treatment if needed.
* Consider a skeletal review, including X-ray of the wrist, hip, spine, and skull, to monitor skeletal development and address any concerns.
* Monitor growth velocity and consider referral for endocrine investigations if height is below the 2nd centile.
* Consider physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and behavioural therapy to support developmental delays and address any concerns.
